title: The hypertrophy series: the optimal number of sets for muscle growth
summary: NH argues there is no universal optimal number of sets (9, 12, 15 or 20 per week) because set count is meaningless without reps, intensity, frequency and individual recovery. He advises starting with the minimum effective number of sets, using evolving set schemes, and letting weight and rep range determine sets rather than reverse engineering.
claims: Now that the 8-12 rep myth has faded, a new myth claims an exact weekly set number for naturals, ranging from 9 to 12 to 15 to 20
A set count is meaningless alone: reps per set, intensity, frequency and how sets are distributed across the week define it
20 sets in one day and 4 sets on each of 5 days are completely different programs
Do as little as possible to get as much as possible: use the minimal number of sets that keeps you progressing and injury-free
When starting to train a body part, begin with about 3 sets per week and move up to 4, 5, 6 only when needed
Doing too much early leads to burnout, no results and a poor relationship with set selection
Some body parts naturally accumulate more sets as a byproduct of the program; forcing one static number for every muscle doesn't work
Body parts differ in size and recovery ability, so set counts should differ by muscle
Evolving set schemes let you progress because you don't always stay at the same number of sets
Going from 3 sets to 1 set lowers volume but raises intensity: with one set you can push much harder and add weight over time
Keeping the same weekly set count for six months is too rigid and limits you
People want certainty from a set prescription; anything works for beginners, but progressing later means accepting risk and uncertainty
20 sets may suit one person and destroy another, and someone who handles 20 may need more later
There is no hard cap on sets, but there is a limit on the usefulness of adding more: with enough sets you manipulate intensity and rep range instead
Adding a 4th set of 6-10 can be productive; adding 5th, 6th, 7th sets means sandbagging, since repeating a rep range that often shows the weight isn't challenging: junk volume
The proper order is choose a weight for a rep range, then let muscular endurance determine sets; picking the set count first and reverse-engineering the weight produces irrelevant loads
Base your set count on your own training experience over time rather than an external number
